interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the arrow made by subtracting two phase arrows, √3 times as long, landing on the line voltage in star and on the line current in delta, when you flip the star–delta switch.
interactive.title: Star and delta
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on one picture. On the left, three supply windings, L1, L2 and L3, each with 230 V across it, are joined in star, and a star point is labelled at their common end; they feed three equal loads through three line conductors. Two lines under the title say 'supply on the left, in star, 230 V a winding' and what the loads are. A switch draws the loads joined in star, with one end of every load meeting at the loads' own labelled star point and a neutral wire, leaving that star point at a slant, back to the supply's, or in delta, with each load joined between two lines in a ring and no star point among the loads. The supply stays in star throughout. A voltmeter and a clamp meter on the drawing are labelled line or phase by where they sit: phase across or through one winding or load, line between two line conductors or round one. On the right are the phasor arrows, frozen at one instant as in Trigonometry's Adding waves with phasors: three phase arrows of equal length, a third of a turn, 120°, apart, and a bold arrow made by subtracting one from the next, which is √3, about 1.732, times as long and turned 30° from them. Each load is a say 23 Ω impedance at a power factor of 0.8, so its current lags its own voltage by 36.9°. Screen 1 shows star: the voltmeter across one winding reads 230 V, and moved between L1 and L2 it reads the bold arrow, L1's arrow minus L2's: 230 × 1.732 = 398.4 V. Screen 2 changes the supply to say 254 V a winding and asks what the voltmeter between L1 and L2 reads: 440 V, from 254 × 1.732 = 439.9 V; 508 V, two phases added as plain numbers (hint: the two phases peak a third of a cycle apart, and the meter reads their difference, not their sum); or 254 V (hint: that is across one winding, line to star point). Its Why? explains that going from L2 to L1 you pass back down L2's winding and up L1's, and that 440 V is the line voltage most ships run. A right Check lays L2's arrow, turned half round, on the tip of L1's and draws the bold arrow closing them; only then does the key show 'an arrow turned half round'. Screen 3 adds the currents in star: each line runs straight into one winding and one load with nothing branching off, so the line current equals the phase current, 230 ÷ 23 = 10 A, drawn as three 10 A arrows each 36.9° behind its voltage. At the star point the three currents meet and return along the neutral, whose arrow is the three current arrows laid tip to tail. Screen 4 asks what the neutral carries with three 10 A phase currents: 0 A, because three equal arrows 120° apart close a triangle; 30 A (hint: the three currents peak at different moments, so they add as arrows, not as numbers); or 10 A (hint: lay them tip to tail; the last tip lands back on the first tail). A right Check slides the three arrows tip to tail into a closed triangle. Its Why? adds that a load that is always balanced can be fed by the three lines alone, and that most ships' main supply is just that, three phases on three wires with no neutral conductor. Screen 5 frees a slider for L3's load current, from 0 to 10 A in steps of 0.5 A, opening at 10 A. As it falls, the triangle no longer closes and the neutral arrow grows from the gap. With L1 and L2 at 10 A, the three phases share an equal part, L3's current, which cancels as before, so what is left is L1's and L2's extra, two equal arrows 120° apart whose sum is one arrow of the same length: the neutral carries 10 A minus L3's current, 4 A when L3 is at 6 A and 10 A when L3 is off. Screen 6 asks what the neutral carries with 10 A, 10 A and 7 A: 3 A; 27 A, the three added as numbers (hint: they are 120° apart, so most of them cancel); or 0 A (hint: only equal currents cancel completely). A right Check sets L3 to 7 A on the slider. Screen 7 flips the switch to delta on the same supply and says that the supply stays in star, so from here phase means one load. Each load now sits between two lines, so its phase voltage is the line voltage, 398.4 V, and it draws 398.4 ÷ 23 = 17.32 A. At the corner where L1 joins, L1 brings the current drawn by the load that starts there, less the current the other load delivers back into that corner, so the clamp on L1 reads the difference of two phase currents 120° apart: the same subtraction, the same bold arrow, now on the currents, 17.32 × 1.732 = 30.0 A. Screen 8 gives other delta loads that each draw 12 A and asks what the clamp on L1 reads: 20.8 A, from 12 × 1.732; 24 A, two phase currents added as plain numbers (hint: they are 120° apart, and L1 carries their difference); or 12 A (hint: that is star's rule; in delta two loads meet at every line). A right Check draws the bold arrow on the current arrows. Screen 9 lights the power readouts and lets the switch be flipped. Each load takes V_ph × I_ph × cos φ, so three take 3 × V_ph × I_ph × cos φ. In star V_ph = V_L ÷ √3 and I_ph = I_L; in delta V_ph = V_L and I_ph = I_L ÷ √3; either way one √3 cancels into the 3, so the two readouts always agree. Every readout is worked from the factors it shows. Star: 3 × 230 × 10 × 0.8 = 5520 W. Delta: 3 × 398.4 × 17.32 × 0.8 = 16,561 W. Screen 10 gives three heaters, 92 Ω each at a power factor of 1, taking 1725 W in star at 2.5 A each, and asks what they take in delta on the same supply: 5175 W, three times, because each has √3 times the voltage and so √3 times the current, 4.33 A; 1725 W (hint: the heaters are the same, but the voltage across each is not); or 2988 W, √3 times (hint: the current through each rises by √3 too). A right Check flips the switch with both readouts in view. Screens 11 to 13 are mixed, drawing on the whole course. Screen 11 gives a load on a board whose line voltage reads, say, 400 V, drawing 20 A a line at a power factor of 0.85, connection unknown, and asks the apparent power its cables carry: 13.9 kVA, from √3 × 400 × 20 = 13,856 VA; 11.8 kVA (hint: that is the true power, the cos φ share; apparent power leaves cos φ out); or 24.0 kVA (hint: 3 goes with phase values; with line values the factor is √3). A right Check shows the volt-amps and then their cos φ share, 13,856 × 0.85 = 11,778 W. Screen 12 gives a delta-connected motor, its three windings drawn as coils between the lines and the supply labelled on the left, whose clamp reads 26 A on one line, and asks the current in each winding: 15.0 A, from 26 ÷ 1.732; 26 A (hint: 26 A is in the line; in delta each line feeds two windings); or 45.0 A (hint: in delta the line carries more than the winding, not less). A right Check draws the bold arrow from two 15.0 A winding currents. Screen 13 shows one cycle of the 400 V line voltage with its rms level marked and asks what peak the insulation between two lines sees: 566 V, from 400 × 1.414, as lesson 2 found the peak of 230 V; 693 V (hint: √3 turns a phase voltage into a line voltage; from rms to peak a sine needs √2); or 400 V (hint: 400 V is the rms; the wave swings higher). A right Check draws the peak arrow. Each puzzle offers three answers; a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, Why? explains in words, and a right Check draws the answer on the picture. Clamp readings are written to the same precision as the text. The closing line says that the √3 comes from subtracting two equal arrows 120° apart, that for a generator star gives the same power with less line current while delta copes better if a winding fails, that a motor's windings are joined in star or delta too, and that the courses after this one take three-phase on to transformers, ships' systems and motors.
interactive.ignores: The supply is drawn holding its voltage whatever the load; a real one sags a little as current rises, and the cables add their own voltage drop. The loads are fixed impedances; a real motor's current and power factor change with how hard it is working. The waves are pure sines; currents with harmonics behave differently in the neutral, as the explanation says. The arrows are frozen at one instant and drawn with rms lengths; the real waves turn and swing. The loads, the 254 V supply, the heaters and their readings are example values.

explain.text:
In its simplest form, a three-phase generator is three of lesson 1's coils on one shaft, set a third of a turn apart,[^1] so they make three equal voltage waves 120° apart. How you join three windings, or three equal loads, decides which reading picks up a factor of √3. Join one end of each at a common point and the voltage between two lines is √3 times the voltage across one. Join them nose to tail in a ring and the current in each line is √3 times the current through one. Either way, the power is √3 × line voltage × line current × power factor.[^3]

Start with the [[star]] connection: one end of every winding meets at the star point, and a line conductor runs from each free end, L1, L2 and L3. Now it matters where you measure. Across one winding, line to star point, a voltmeter reads the phase voltage, 230 V on UK mains.[^2] Between two lines it reads the [[line voltage]]. Going from L2 to L1 you pass back down L2's winding and up L1's, so the line voltage is L1's arrow minus L2's, found by adding L2's arrow turned half round,[^4] as in Trigonometry's Adding waves with phasors. Two equal arrows 120° apart differ by an arrow √3 times as long, so the line voltage is 230 × 1.732 = 398.4 V, close to the 400 V you read between lines at a board. Each line runs straight into one winding with nothing branching off, so the line current is the phase current.[^5] Say each load is 23 Ω at a power factor of 0.8: each phase carries 230 ÷ 23 = 10 A. The three currents meet at the star point and return along the neutral. Laid tip to tail, three equal arrows 120° apart close a triangle, so a balanced load leaves the neutral carrying nothing,[^6] and a load that is always balanced can be fed by the three lines alone. Most ships' main supply is just that: a marine engineering text describes the usual ship's system as three-phase, three-wire, 440 V, with no neutral conductor run.[^10] Drop L3 to 5 A and the equal part, 5 A in each phase, still cancels; what is left is L1's and L2's extra 5 A, two equal arrows 120° apart whose sum is one 5 A arrow. So the neutral carries 5 A, not 25 A. That cancelling is for sine-wave currents: currents with harmonics at three times the supply frequency add in the neutral instead.[^7]

In [[delta]], each load is joined between two lines, in a ring. The supply stays in star, so from here phase means one load. Each load has the line voltage across it: the phase voltage is the line voltage, 398.4 V, and each 23 Ω load draws 398.4 ÷ 23 = 17.32 A. At the corner where L1 joins, L1 brings the current drawn by the load that starts there, less the current the other load delivers back into that corner. So L1 carries the difference of two phase currents 120° apart. It is the same subtraction, now on currents: 17.32 × 1.732 = 30.0 A. The √3 has moved from the voltage to the current, and with no star point among the loads there is no neutral to them. A US Navy training problem has a 450 V three-phase system supplying a delta-connected 100 hp load at a power factor of 0.92 lagging:[^11] each phase of that load has the full 450 V across it. For a generator's own windings there is a trade-off: delta gives "greater reliability in the event of winding failure", while star can deliver "the same amount of power with less line current".[^9] A motor's three windings are joined in these same two ways, which the Machines and drives course takes up.

Each load takes V_ph × I_ph × cos φ, lesson 8's true power,[^8] where φ is the angle inside that load between its own voltage and current. Three loads take 3 V_ph I_ph cos φ. In star, V_ph = V_L ÷ √3 and I_ph = I_L; in delta, V_ph = V_L and I_ph = I_L ÷ √3. Either way one √3 divides into the 3 and leaves √3 V_L I_L cos φ,[^3] so for a balanced load line readings give the power without your knowing the connection. Star: 3 × 230 × 10 × 0.8 = 5520 W. The same loads in delta take 3 × 398.4 × 17.32 × 0.8 = 16,561 W, three times as much but for rounding, because each has √3 times the voltage and so √3 times the current. This is a simplified model, with balanced loads, pure sine waves and a supply that holds its voltage. As in lesson 8's motor example, each phase has its own power triangle, so three-phase cables carry √3 V_L I_L volt-amps, of which only the cos φ share arrives as watts. **In star the line voltage is √3 times the phase voltage and the line current equals the phase current;[^5] in delta the √3 moves to the current; either way three equal loads take √3 V_L I_L cos φ.[^3]**

analogy.text: Three crew haul on lines shackled to one ring, a third of the way round from each other. Pulling equally, their pulls cancel and the ring's anchor feels nothing, as a balanced load leaves the neutral at zero. Ease off one line to half and the anchor takes a pull equal to that missing half, towards the other two, as the neutral takes the 5 A one phase has dropped.
analogy.breaks: The crew pull steadily, while phase currents swing to and fro fifty or sixty times a second, so the neutral's current is a wave too, not a steady pull. And the ring tells you nothing about the √3 between star and delta, which comes from subtracting arrows, not from adding them.

practice.text:
- Safety first: between two lines there is the line voltage, about 400 V on a UK board, not 230 V.
- Say where you are measuring: line (between two line conductors, or the current in one) or phase (across one winding or load, or the current through it).
- Find the connection. Star has a star point, often with a neutral; delta has none.
- Star: V_ph = V_L ÷ √3 and I_ph = I_L. Delta: V_ph = V_L and I_ph = I_L ÷ √3.
- Power: P = √3 × V_L × I_L × cos φ,[^3] with cos φ the load's own power factor.
- Check it with phase values: 3 × V_ph × I_ph × cos φ gives the same.

**Rules of thumb:** √3 is about 1.732. A balanced load of sine-wave currents leaves the neutral at nearly nothing;[^6] a large neutral current usually means unbalance or harmonics.[^7] A line voltage is rms like any label: just as 230 V peaks at about 325 V,[^12] 400 V between lines peaks at 400 × 1.414 = 566 V. Fixed loads such as heaters, moved from star to delta on the same supply, take three times the power; a motor's power is set by what it drives.

**Worked example:** A star-connected load on a board reading 400 V between lines draws 12 A a line at a power factor of 0.9. Each phase has 400 ÷ 1.732 = 230.9 V across it and carries 12 A. Power: √3 × 400 × 12 × 0.9 = 7482 W, about 7.48 kW. Check: 3 × 230.9 × 12 × 0.9 = 7481 W, the same but for rounding.

**Common mistakes**
- Adding two phase voltages as numbers, 460 V. They are 120° apart; the line voltage is their difference, √3 times one.
- Using 3 with line values, or √3 with phase values.
- Taking φ as the angle between a line voltage and a line current. In star a line voltage is turned 30° from its phase voltages, so between L1's current and the L1–L2 voltage the angle is φ + 30°, not φ.
- Expecting the neutral to carry the three currents added. It carries what fails to cancel.
- Thinking star or delta makes no difference to the power. On the same supply, delta puts √3 times the voltage on each load.
